newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thais must attract funds to ease woes-economist.
newsitem.headline: Thais must attract funds to ease woes-economist.

text.p: Thailand must act urgently to attract funds and raise liquidity in the system to deal with current economic woes, a leading economist said on Monday.

Kenneth Courtis, chief economist and strategist of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo, said the authorities should boost liquidity by deregulating the country's foreign equity participation law, issuing legislation that facilitates securitisation and launching a financial institutions stabilisation programme.

With improved liquidity, Thailand will be able to bring down high interest rates, alleviate problems in the property and finance sectors and prevent them from spilling over into the overall economy, he told reporters.
"If you get that...then you can start moving interest rates down and you don't have to worry that the whole thing will blow up in your face," Courtis said.
"The longer the measures are delayed, the higher the cost will be," he said.

Thailand's latest efforts to solve its financial problems hit snags on Monday when the government decided to delay approval of planned royal decrees on guidelines for finance company mergers and conversion of loans and assets into securities.
The delay was caused by a request by the new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya who said he needed more time to study the planned decrees.
Troubles in the cash-strapped property sector and bearish short-term sentiment about the Thai economic outlook have hurt the country's liquidity situation.
An inflexible baht system, which has forced the authorities to keep interest rates high to defend it even when the country is facing its lowest economic growth in a decade, has made matters worse.
The baht, which is pegged against various currencies in a trade-weighted basket, has come under sporadic speculative attacks since late last year on devaluation talk.
The Thai authorities have tried in the past to push for cuts in lending rates to resuscitate the economy, but the recent attacks on the baht have limited the scope for any cut.

Analysts said Thailand would need to use a lot of public funds to bail out the finance and property sectors. However, some current legislation imposes limitations on Thailand's ability to raise funds.
Thai law now limits foreign equity participation in finance companies and commercial banks to only 25 percent.
Courtis said this inhibited foreign buyers from entering the Thai market to take stakes in firms.

"Foreign investors could buy real estate by buying the equity of the finance companies (which suffered overexposure to the property sector) and taking over their underlying assets," he added. However, despite the ongoing economic malaise, he was confident about the long-term prospects of the Thai economy.
